Pipeline for PICRUSt2 standard output

standard-pipeline.Rmd

A standard PICRUSt2 table gives one predicted abundance for each function in each sample. It is a natural starting point when your question is about the community as a whole. Which pathways differ between groups, or which samples have similar functional profiles?

We keep this workflow at the community level. A pathway difference in this table does not tell us which taxon produced it. If your next question is about the contributors, keep the standard analysis as context and continue with the stratified workflow.

Generate PICRUSt2 standard (community-level) output

PICRUSt2 takes representative sequences (FASTA) and a feature table (BIOM/TSV) as input and produces predicted functional profiles at the community level (unstratified).
If you need installation instructions, see the official documentation.

1.1 Inputs

Prepare the following inputs. - dna-sequences.fasta — representative sequences (ASVs/OTUs) - feature-table.biom — counts table (features × samples)

picrust2_pipeline.py \
  -s dna-sequences.fasta \
  -i feature-table.biom \
  -o picrust2_out \
  -p 8

Key outputs you will use

  • picrust2_out/KO_metagenome_out/pred_metagenome_unstrat.tsv

  • picrust2_out/EC_metagenome_out/pred_metagenome_unstrat.tsv

  • picrust2_out/pathways_out/path_abun_unstrat.tsv

Each file is a feature × sample matrix (first column = feature ID, remaining columns = samples).

Choose the level that answers your question

Individual KOs and pathways describe different resolutions. Converting KO abundance to a KEGG pathway table is helpful when you want a pathway-level summary, but it changes the unit you are comparing. A KO may map to more than one pathway, so pathway totals should not be read as mutually exclusive pieces of one conserved total.

Prepare a KO abundance matrix

For ko2kegg_abundance(data = ...), use a data frame whose first column contains KO IDs, followed by sample abundance columns.

library(MicroFun)
data("ko_abundance", package = "MicroFun")
data("metadata", package = "MicroFun")
kegg_abundance <- ko2kegg_abundance(data = ko_abundance)

This conversion uses the bundled local KO-to-KEGG pathway mapping and does not contact KEGG. To use your own local membership file, pass kegg_map to ko2kegg_abundance(). Online annotation in the next section is a separate step and does not refresh this mapping. See mapping and network access for the reference-data details.

Once the table is ready, check that its sample columns match the metadata. A correctly shaped matrix can still describe the wrong comparison if sample identifiers have been lost or reordered.

Fit community-level differential abundance 

daa_results_df <- pathway_daa(
  abundance = kegg_abundance, metadata = metadata,
  group = "Environment", daa_method = "LinDA"
)
daa_annotated_results_df <- pathway_annotation(
  pathway = "KO", daa_results_df = daa_results_df, ko_to_kegg = TRUE
)

The pathway_annotation() call above requires a KEGG connection and the KEGGREST package. MicroFun sends the requests automatically. Academic users do not need to apply for or supply an API key.

The model asks about group-associated differences in the selected functional features. Choose a method that fits the type and scale of your input, and inspect the returned feature IDs, group labels and adjusted p-values before making a figure. Annotation gives those IDs biological context; it does not change the underlying statistical test.

Use one method and one contrast for each result plot. For error bars, match sample groups to abundance columns by sample ID before passing Group.

Visualize sample-level profiles

Follow the shared setup and Community-level visualizations for PCA, row-standardized heatmaps, annotated error bars and metagenome correlation comparisons.

The error-bar ratio is a descriptive log2 ratio of group means; its direction depends on the first factor level. It is different from the signed MaAsLin2 AST coefficients used in stratified association plots.

The standard demonstration study is reserved for the forthcoming figures and analysis.

What should a result mean?

Read a selected pathway alongside its abundance distribution and the direction of the comparison. A small adjusted p-value alone does not tell you whether the difference is large, consistent across samples or driven by a few unusual observations. The Community-level visualizations guide provides several views that help you examine those possibilities.

These profiles are predictions derived from 16S information and reference genomes. They describe inferred functional potential; they do not directly measure gene expression or metabolic activity.
